bib.title: ArcMemo: Abstract Reasoning Composition with Lifelong LLM Memory

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "ArcMemo: Abstract Reasoning Composition with Lifelong LLM Memory", Matthew Ho, Chen Si, Zhaoxiang Feng, Fangxu Yu, Yichi Yang, Zhijian Liu, Zhiting Hu, Lianhui Qin (UCSD, UMD). arXiv 2509.04439v3, 4 Oct 2025. Venue: every page header reads "Preprint."; no conference acceptance appears in the text. Code: github.com/matt-seb-ho/arc_memo.
COVERAGE: 55,180 of 55,180 chars read (all pages, main text, Tables 1-5, Appendices A-E, references). Figures 1-4 are images and were not viewed; only the text around them was read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Concept-level memory beats a no-memory baseline modestly, and only the PS (program-synthesis) format does so at every compute scale.
 number: 55.17 to 59.33 official score (+7.5% relative)
 setup: ARC-AGI-1, random 100-puzzle subset of the public validation split, o4-mini (medium), program-synthesis evaluation, 3 runs averaged, oracle@2, 0 retries, memory fixed (frozen), seeded with 160 hand-written solutions.
 quote: "our method improves the official score from 55.17 to 59.33 (+7.5% relative gain over a strong no-memory baseline) and is the only memory design we find to outperform the baseline at all inference scales."
 where: Intro, p.2; Table 1, p.8
2. The gain is within noise at some settings. The baseline std is 3.18, against 0.29 for PS. At retry 2 the baseline (69.00) is close to PS (70.83), and the cheatsheet (71.33) is higher. At retry 1 the baseline (66.67) is only 0.66 below PS (67.33).
 number: PS 59.33 (0.29) vs baseline 55.17 (3.18) at retry 0; retry 2: PS 70.83 vs baseline 69.00 vs cheatsheet 71.33
 setup: as above, Table 4, oracle@2.
 quote: "ArcMemo-PS's advantage is most prominent with lower compute regimes... The marginal impact of memory is reduced with more inference compute as the model can rediscover ideas through exploration."
 where: Sec 5.1, p.8; Table 4, p.13
3. Abstract, modular concepts were chosen over instance-level or whole-summary memory. Instance-level entries "have diminished utility for problems superficially different from prior experiences". Raw instance memory is not itself tested as an arm. The only comparators are no memory and a Dynamic Cheatsheet re-implementation (a single rewritten summary).
 number: OE 56.67, PS 59.33, cheatsheet 57.67, baseline 55.17 (oracle@2, retry 0)
 quote: "ArcMemo-OE (ours, o4-mini (medium)) 48.00 (1.00) 56.67 (1.53)" and "ArcMemo-PS (ours, o4-mini (medium)) 49.33 (0.29) 59.33 (0.29)"
 where: Table 1, p.8
4. Selecting a subset of memory helps and costs fewer tokens than injecting all of it.
 number: 59.33 vs 55.17 (no selection) at retry 0; at retries 1 and 2 the gap shrinks to 1.3 and 0.8
 setup: ArcMemo-PS with the reasoning-based selection removed, same model and subset.
 quote: "- selection 46.83 (5.25) 55.17 (2.02) 60.00"
 where: Table 2, p.8
 Also: "the selection-ablated setting uses far more tokens" (Fig 4). In Appendix C: "memory-augmented runs tend to increase output token usage", so token efficiency is "similar to the baseline".
5. Attribution check: only 40% of the cheatsheet's new solves trace to its content, against 100% for ArcMemo-PS without selection.
 number: 40% vs 100%; 10 differing puzzles (5 each)
 quote: "only 40% of new solves in the cheatsheet setting were related to memory elements actually in the generated cheatsheet." / "100% of new solves from ArcMemo-PS (-selection) can be linked to concept memory contents."
 setup: manual analysis by the authors, a handful of puzzles; they say causation cannot be concluded.
 where: Sec 5.2, p.9
6. Continual updating during evaluation helps only at deeper retries, and the results are mixed. This is ArcMemo-OE, updating every 10 problems with self-generated solutions.
 number: retry 2 oracle@2: 67.67 to 70.00. At retry 0 it falls 56.67 to 56.00, and at retry 1 it falls 65.67 to 65.00.
 quote: "+ continual memory update62.33 (3.51) 70.00 (1.73) 72.00"
 where: Table 3, p.9
 Side finding: embedding retrieval was poor and "lowering the score from 0.26 to 0.22, marking a 15% reduction" (o3-mini, Appx C, p.14).

BASELINES AND COMPUTE MATCHING
- Baselines: (a) no memory, o4-mini medium. (b) Cheatsheet, a re-implementation of Dynamic Cheatsheet DC-Cu (Suzgun et al. 2025) with frozen memory. (c) Other models for context (Table 1): qwen3-235b 16.67, deepseek r1 26.33, claude sonnet 4 54.17, gemini 2.5 flash 13.83.
- Compute is matched on the number of attempts, not on tokens. Memory and baseline get the same oracle@k, the same retries and the same parallel samples. Output tokens are not equalized: memory runs use more output tokens (Appx C), and the extra tokens for the abstraction and selection calls (GPT-4.1 and a reasoning model) are not obviously charged. There is no baseline given extra samples to equal the memory's total token budget. Fig 4 plots score against reasoning tokens.
- The paper treats memory benefit as shrinking with compute, which is the compute-matched story. At retry 2 and 3 parallel samples the baseline is nearly equal (73.00 vs 75.50, k=3).
- Strict scoring (Table 5, a single program must solve all test cases) gives similar numbers: PS 59.00 vs baseline 54.67 at retry 0.

LIMITS (authors and observed)
- Only 100 puzzles from ARC-AGI-1; high sampling variance; only 3 runs. The authors concede this "limit[s] the absolute magnitude of observable gains".
- ARC-AGI-2 not run. One main model (o4-mini); o3-mini only for the embedding test.
- Needs a test-time feedback signal (test cases) to decide which traces to store. Incorrect traces are not used, and credit assignment is left open.
- The main comparisons use frozen memory seeded from 160 human-written solutions (Li et al. 2024). That is external expert data, not self-learned experience. The continual-update test used OE only, not PS.
- Order dependence and batching trade-off with continual updates. The memory is flat, with no consolidation.
- The concept-specificity test (n=10) shows tension: more specific concepts solve more (4/10 at maximum detail) but are harder to retrieve.
- Transfer is argued from the design (Fig 1) and not tested directly. No cross-domain or unseen-concept transfer test; the 100 evaluation puzzles come from the same benchmark family as the seeds.

BUILDS ON
Suzgun et al. 2025 (Dynamic Cheatsheet); Yang et al. 2024 (Buffer of Thoughts); Liu et al. 2023 (Think-in-Memory); Park et al. 2023 (Generative Agents); Wang et al. 2023a (Voyager); Shinn et al. 2023 (Reflexion); Liu et al. 2025 (Contextual Experience Replay); Fang et al. 2025 (MemP, concurrent, "Work in progress"); Lewis et al. 2021 (RAG); Packer et al. 2024 (MemGPT); Chhikara et al. 2025 (Mem0); Li et al. 2024 (seed solutions); Akyürek et al. 2025 (100-puzzle subset, test-time training); Wang et al. 2024 (hypothesis search); Qiu et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2024 and Kamoi et al. 2024 (self-correction needs external feedback). The references give arXiv IDs, mostly without venues.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
Figure 1 (p.2), "Instance-Level vs. Abstract Concepts Example." It shows why composed rules (A∧B⇒C) transfer poorly and modular concepts recombine. It is the clearest picture of the raw-vs-distilled argument. The figure itself was not viewed; the caption was read from the text extraction.

PROBLEMS: none blocking. No embedded instructions found. Table text is flattened by extraction but readable.
